lessons.title: Choosing Cameras and Gimbals for Drones
lessons.body: When choosing a camera for your drone, start with the sensor size. For most African conditions, a 1-inch sensor (like on the DJI Air 3) handles bright sun and shadows better than a small 1/2.3-inch sensor. If you're on a budget, the DJI Mini 4 Pro has a 1/1.3-inch sensor and shoots 4K/60fps. For professional work, the DJI Mavic 3 Pro has a 4/3 CMOS sensor and adjustable aperture. In Africa, dust and heat are real: choose a camera with a sealed lens or buy a UV filter to protect it. Gimbals: most drones have built-in 3-axis gimbals. If you're building a custom rig, the Gremsy T3 or Tarot TL3T01 are popular for DSLR cameras. But for beginners, a ready-to-fly drone like the DJI Mini 4 Pro or Autel EVO Lite+ is best. Check that the gimbal can tilt from -90Â° (straight down) to +30Â° (upward) for versatile shots. Also consider storage: 4K video eats 350MB per minute. Buy a 128GB microSD card (SanDisk Extreme) and format it in the drone. In hot African climates, avoid leaving the drone in a car; heat can damage the gimbal motors. Test your gimbal by calibrating it in the app before each flight. If you see jitter, recalibrate. For night shots, a gimbal with a wide aperture (f/2.8) helps. Remember, the camera and gimbal work together; a good gimbal stabilizes even in 20 km/h wind. Practice smooth tilts and pans manually before relying on automated modes.

lessons.title: Camera Settings: Aperture, Shutter Speed, ISO
lessons.body: Aperture controls how much light hits the sensor. A low f-number (f/2.8) lets in more light and blurs the background; a high f-number (f/11) keeps everything sharp. For aerial landscapes, use f/5.6 to f/8 for a sharp horizon. Shutter speed: for photos, use 1/500s or faster to freeze motion if you're moving. For video, the 180-degree rule says shutter speed should be double your frame rate. So at 30fps, use 1/60s; at 60fps, use 1/120s. This gives natural motion blur. ISO: keep it as low as possible. In bright African sun, ISO 100. In overcast or dusk, ISO 400-800. Above ISO 1600, you'll see noise. Use ND filters to control light without changing aperture. For example, a PolarPro ND8 or ND16 filter lets you use f/5.6 and 1/60s in bright sun. White balance: set manually to 5600K for daylight, 3200K for golden hour. Don't use autoâit shifts mid-video. For photos, shoot RAW for more editing flexibility. For video, use D-Log M or flat profiles if you plan to color grade. But if you're delivering straight out of camera, use Normal profile. Test your settings before a paid shoot: take a 10-second clip at different ISOs and check on a laptop. In dusty conditions, avoid changing lenses; use a fixed-lens drone. Practice in your backyard: set f/5.6, 1/60s, ISO 100, and adjust from there. Always check your histogramânot just the screenâbecause bright African skies can fool you.

lessons.title: Aerial Composition and Framing
lessons.body: Aerial composition is about guiding the viewer's eye. Use the rule of thirds: imagine a 3x3 grid and place your subject on an intersection. For example, a lone acacia tree in the Serengeti looks better on the left third, not dead center. Leading lines: roads, rivers, or fences draw the eye. In African cities like Nairobi or Lagos, use roads to lead to a building. Symmetry: shoot straight down at a market or a roundabout for a geometric look. But avoid boring top-downs; tilt the gimbal to 45Â° for depth. Foreground, midground, background: include a near object (a branch, a rock) to add scale. For example, when filming a waterfall, start with a close-up of rocks, then reveal the falls. Lighting: shoot during golden hour (first hour after sunrise, last hour before sunset) for warm light and long shadows. Avoid midday harsh light unless you want high contrast. In the bush, use shadows to frame animals. Keep the horizon level: use the drone's grid lines or a bubble level. If you're filming a moving subject (a car, a herd), use active track and keep the subject in the same third of the frame. For video, start with a wide establishing shot, then move closer. Don't zoomâfly closer. For photos, bracket exposures: take three shots at -1, 0, +1 EV and merge in post. Practice by flying at 50m altitude and composing a scene with a single tree. Then try a village scene: include a person for scale. Always check edges of the frameâdon't cut off buildings or heads. In Africa, respect local customs: don't fly over people without permission, and avoid sacred sites.

lessons.title: Capturing Smooth Video: Techniques and Settings
lessons.body: Smooth video starts with smooth flying. Use Tripod mode (DJI) or Cinematic mode (Autel) to slow down controls. Set expo curves to 0.25 for gentle stick response. Practice flying figure-eights and orbits without touching the yaw. For a reveal shot, fly backward while tilting the gimbal down slowly. For a fly-through, fly forward at 2 m/s and keep the gimbal level. Use the 180-degree shutter rule: at 30fps, set shutter to 1/60s. If it's too bright, use an ND filter (ND8 or ND16). In African sun, you'll often need ND16 or ND32. For smooth pans, use the gimbal's pan axis, not the drone's yawâit's smoother. Set gimbal speed to slow (10-20%) and smoothness to 20. For tracking shots, use ActiveTrack 360Â° (DJI) or Dynamic Track (Autel). But don't rely on it for fast subjects; manual is better. Fly in calm conditions: wind above 20 km/h causes jitter. Check UAV Forecast app. For hyperlapse, set interval to 2 seconds, speed 2 m/s, and duration 12 seconds. For slow-motion, shoot at 120fps and interpret at 24fps. Always record in 4K, even if you deliver 1080pâyou can crop. Use a flat profile (D-Log M) for more dynamic range, but only if you color grade. Otherwise, use Normal. Keep your footage organized: format card before each shoot, name folders by date and location. After flight, review clips on a laptop; delete bad ones. Practice a 30-second sequence: start wide, push in, orbit, tilt up to reveal. Do this 10 times until it's muscle memory.

lessons.title: Post-Processing: Editing Aerial Footage
lessons.body: For editing, start with free or affordable tools: DaVinci Resolve (free) or Adobe Premiere Pro (subscription). On a laptop, use proxies for 4K footage. Import your clips, then create a timeline. First, color correct: adjust exposure, contrast, and white balance. For African skies, bring down highlights and lift shadows. Use scopes: keep luminance between 0 and 100 IRE. For D-Log M footage, apply a LUT (DJI provides free LUTs). Then color grade: add warmth to golden hour shots, cool tones to overcast. For photos, edit in Lightroom or Snapseed. Use dehaze to cut through dust, and vibrance to boost colors without oversaturation. For video stabilization, use Warp Stabilizer in Premiere or Stabilization in Resolve. But don't overdo itâcrop in slightly. For smooth transitions, use cross dissolves or whip pans. Add music: use royalty-free tracks from Epidemic Sound or YouTube Audio Library. Keep it simple: cut on action, not on every beat. Export at 4K, H.264, 20-50 Mbps. For social media, export 1080p. Always back up your footage to two drives. In Africa, power can be unreliableâuse a UPS. For a 1-minute video, expect 2-3 hours of editing. Practice with a 10-clip project: trim, color, add music, export. Watch tutorials on YouTube for specific techniques like sky replacement or tracking. Remember, editing is where good footage becomes great. Don't skip it.

lessons.title: Legal and Commercial Aspects of Aerial Media
lessons.body: Before flying commercially in any African country, check local drone laws. In Kenya, you need a Remote Pilot License (RPL) from the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) and an Operator Certificate. In South Africa, register with SACAA and get an RPL. In Nigeria, the NCAA requires a permit. In many countries, flying without a license can lead to fines or confiscation. For commercial work, you need insurance: public liability and hull coverage. In Kenya, providers like AAR or Jubilee offer drone insurance. For pricing, a typical real estate shoot (30 photos, 1-minute video) in Nairobi costs KES 20,000-50,000. In Lagos, NGN 100,000-200,000. For a wedding, KES 30,000-60,000. Always have a contract: specify deliverables, timeline, and usage rights. For social media, charge extra for raw footage. For stock footage, upload to Artgrid or Pond5âyou earn 30-50% commission. But avoid flying over crowds, airports, or military bases. In wildlife areas, get permits from KWS (Kenya) or SANParks (South Africa). For privacy, don't film people without consent, especially in rural areas. For commercial real estate, get permission from the property owner. Keep a flight log: date, location, duration, and purpose. This helps with audits. Also, register your drone with the local authority. In Tanzania, you need a permit from TCAA. Always carry your license and insurance when flying. For cross-border work, check if your license is recognized. Join local drone associations like the African Drone Alliance for support. Remember, legal compliance builds trust and avoids fines.

quiz.q: Which sensor size is recommended for handling bright sun and shadows in African conditions?
quiz.explanation: A 1-inch sensor handles bright sun and shadows better than smaller sensors.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of a gimbal that tilts from -90Â° to +30Â°?
options: A) It allows straight-down and upward shots
quiz.explanation: A tilt range of -90Â° to +30Â° enables versatile shots from straight down to slightly upward.

quiz.q: How much storage does 4K video typically consume per minute?
quiz.explanation: 4K video eats about 350MB per minute.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid leaving a drone in a car in hot African climates?
options: A) It can damage the gimbal motors
quiz.explanation: Heat can damage the gimbal motors.

quiz.q: What is the 180-degree rule for shutter speed in video?
options: A) Shutter speed should be double the frame rate
B) Shutter speed should equal the frame rate
C) Shutter speed should be half the frame rate
D) Shutter speed should be 1/1000s always
quiz.explanation: The 180-degree rule states shutter speed should be double the frame rate for natural motion blur.

quiz.q: What ISO should you use in bright African sun?
quiz.explanation: In bright sun, keep ISO as low as possible, typically 100.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an ND filter?
options: A) To control light without changing aperture
quiz.explanation: ND filters reduce light entering the lens, allowing you to use wider apertures or slower shutter speeds.

quiz.q: What white balance setting is recommended for daylight?
quiz.explanation: 5600K is standard for daylight.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid auto white balance for video?
quiz.explanation: Auto white balance can shift mid-video, causing color inconsistencies.

quiz.q: What is the rule of thirds?
options: A) Place subject on intersection of 3x3 grid
quiz.explanation: The rule of thirds suggests placing subjects on the intersections of a 3x3 grid for better composition.

quiz.q: What is a leading line in aerial composition?
options: A) A road or river that draws the eye
B) A cable connecting drone to controller
D) A type of lens flare
quiz.explanation: Leading lines like roads or rivers guide the viewer's eye through the image.

quiz.q: When is golden hour for aerial photography?
options: A) First hour after sunrise and last hour before sunset
quiz.explanation: Golden hour is the first hour after sunrise and last hour before sunset, offering warm light.

quiz.q: What should you do to keep the horizon level?
options: A) Use grid lines or a bubble level
quiz.explanation: Grid lines or a bubble level help keep the horizon level.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for composing a scene with a single tree?
options: A) Place it on a third
quiz.explanation: Placing the tree on a third follows the rule of thirds for better composition.

quiz.q: What mode should you use for smooth flying?
quiz.explanation: Tripod or Cinematic mode slows down controls for smoother flying.

quiz.q: What expo curve setting is recommended for gentle stick response?
quiz.explanation: An expo curve of 0.25 gives gentle stick response.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gimbal speed for smooth pans?
quiz.explanation: A gimbal speed of 10-20% ensures smooth pans.

quiz.q: What wind speed causes jitter in video?
quiz.explanation: Wind above 20 km/h causes jitter in footage.

quiz.q: What is the interval for a hyperlapse?
quiz.explanation: A 2-second interval is common for hyperlapse.

quiz.q: What frame rate should you shoot for slow-motion?
quiz.explanation: Shooting at 120fps allows slow-motion when interpreted at 24fps.

quiz.q: Which software is free for editing aerial footage?
quiz.explanation: DaVinci Resolve has a free version.

quiz.q: What should you use for 4K footage on a laptop?
quiz.explanation: Proxies are lower-resolution files that make editing 4K smoother.

quiz.q: What does dehaze do in photo editing?
quiz.explanation: Dehaze reduces atmospheric haze and dust effects.

quiz.q: What is a good export bitrate for 4K video?
quiz.explanation: 20-50 Mbps is a good balance for 4K H.264 export.

quiz.q: Why should you back up footage to two drives?
quiz.explanation: Backing up to two drives prevents data loss from drive failure.

quiz.q: What license is needed for commercial drone flying in Kenya?
options: A) Remote Pilot License (RPL) from KCAA
quiz.explanation: In Kenya, a Remote Pilot License from KCAA is required.

quiz.q: What insurance is recommended for commercial drone work?
options: A) Public liability and hull coverage
quiz.explanation: Public liability and hull coverage protect against damage and injury.

quiz.q: What is a typical price for a real estate drone shoot in Nairobi?
quiz.explanation: A typical real estate shoot in Nairobi costs KES 20,000-50,000.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a flight log?
quiz.explanation: A flight log helps with audits and regulatory compliance.

quiz.q: What should you avoid when flying commercially?
quiz.explanation: Flying over crowds is unsafe and often illegal.
